clue.text: Ring — epic works involving singer? This describes it

definitions.text: Ring — epic works involving singer? This describes it

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap round the singer, taking it in
the word epic is worked over, its letters rearranged

parts.note: a singer is slang for an informer, a rat who sings to the police

explanation.surface: A question about Wagner's Ring cycle: an epic work with singers, and what word sums it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singer' is slang for an informer, one who sings to the police. 'works' rearranges the word epic to PEIC around the singer. The whole clue also defines: the Ring is a cycle of operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's Ring cycle is a set of four operas, so the adjective for opera describes it exactly.

clue.text: Stupid or wise?

definitions.meaning: owl-like can mean dull and blinking, slow on the uptake
the owl is a traditional symbol of wisdom, so owl-like means looking sage

explanation.surface: Asks whether a person is dim or clever.
explanation.definitionFit: Owlish describes someone who looks like an owl: solemn and wise-seeming, or blinking and dull.

clue.text: Stretch of river fed by basins

indicators.note: fed by means taking something in, so the river has the basins put inside it

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a crossword favourite
pans are basins, as in salt pans

explanation.surface: A length of river that is fed by basins of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch of river' looks like one phrase, but only 'Stretch' is the definition; the Exe is a river in Devon, and 'fed by' puts the basins inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide area or stretch of land, sea or sky.

clue.text: Upset one man with Lab, out walking

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and thrown into disorder, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A man and his Labrador go out walking, but one of them is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges I, MAN, LAB and OUT. 'Lab' is the dog, not a laboratory, and is fodder either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambulation is the formal word for moving about on foot.

clue.text: Popular writer's wearing fur after initially deeming it essential

indicators.note: after means the fur piece is written following the earlier letters

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable

indicators.note: initially takes the first letters of deeming and it
wearing means having on, so the fur goes around the writers

parts.note: sable is a valuable fur
a pen is a writer; with the apostrophe s it makes the plural

explanation.surface: A popular author in fur believes it a must-have.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes D and I; 'wearing' puts the writers inside the fur, and 'after' places that piece last. The apostrophe s in writer's makes a plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indispensable cannot be done without, as a vital part.

clue.text: Harry Potter's first audio-book?

indicators.note: the first letter of Potter's is taken
audio marks that the book is to be heard, so its sound gives the letters

parts.note: Esther is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: Asks whether there is an audiobook of the first Harry Potter novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry Potter' looks like the boy wizard, but Harry is a verb, the definition. ESTHER said aloud sounds like ESTER, written after P.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to harass or keep bothering them, the same as nagging at them.

clue.text: Pound perhaps will be unknown in time

indicators.note: in means put inside the period of time

parts.note: an era is a period of time
Z is an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: Someone's weight will be unknown for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money or weight, but it names the poet Ezra Pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra Pound was the American modernist poet, so Ezra is an example of a Pound's first name.

clue.text: Bar tab originally an extortionate price

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of tab

parts.note: a ransom is a heavy price extorted for release

explanation.surface: A drinks bill at the bar comes to a scandalous sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'tab' look like a pub bill; Bar is the definition, a crosspiece.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal crossbar, as above a door or window.

clue.text: Payment, including interest, for dwelling

indicators.note: including means holding inside, so the interest goes within the payment

parts.note: rent is a regular payment for a home
a side is an interest or aspect, as in a side of one's life

explanation.surface: Paying rent plus interest for a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interest' looks financial but means an aspect, as in the side of an argument; 'including' puts it inside the payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Resident as an adjective means living in a place, so it means the same as dwelling.

clue.text: Drink Bud, knocking it back

indicators.note: knocking back reads as turning the word round, the friend's name written backwards

parts.note: bud is American slang for a pal or friend

explanation.surface: Someone downs a Budweiser beer in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: Bud looks like the beer, but it is a friend, PAL; 'knocking it back' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap is to drink by scooping liquid with the tongue, as a cat does with milk.

clue.text: Times when it all goes wrong, diary has suggested ?

definitions.text: Times when it all goes wrong

parts.note: the answer's own words act as an instruction: the first word signals an anagram of the rest, and that anagram is what the clue's words diary has spell

explanation.surface: Someone's diary has foreseen the days when everything goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse idea: read the answer as wordplay and BAD is an anagram signal on HAIRDAYS, which rearranges to DIARY HAS. The question mark stands for the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad hair day is an idiom for a day when nothing goes right, starting with unruly hair.

clue.text: A useless supporter, in a ho-hum way

parts.note: pathetic means hopeless or useless
an ally is a supporter

explanation.surface: A hopeless backer cheers the team on with no enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with no interest or enthusiasm is acting with indifference, which ho-hum conveys.

clue.text: Lonely hearts' venue is a blessing in disguise, right?

indicators.note: something in disguise has its look changed, so these letters are rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: Wonders if a lonely hearts' meeting place might be a blessing in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a blessing in disguise' is a set phrase, but 'in disguise' is the anagram signal on A BLESSING, giving SINGLESBA before R.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar aimed at unattached people looking to meet a partner is where lonely hearts might go.

clue.text: Spend regularly on uniform that's second-hand

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word Spend

explanation.surface: Advice to spend now and then on a uniform bought pre-owned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes S, E, D from Spend, placed after U, which is what 'on' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes that were worn by someone before you are second-hand, or not new.

clue.text: Government cuts exposed twice — know what I mean?

indicators.note: twice means the result is written two times over
cuts means slices into, so the government letter goes inside

parts.note: exposed means naked, nude

explanation.surface: Government cuts are revealed, with a knowing hint about what they mean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts' puts G inside NUDE; 'twice' repeats it. The answer is the Monty Python catchphrase hinting at innuendo.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase is said with a wink to hint at a saucy double meaning, as is the definition.

clue.text: Dictator's lead perhaps shows courage

indicators.note: a dictator is someone who speaks words for writing down, so this signals the sound of a word

parts.note: lead is one example of a metal

explanation.surface: A tyrant's leadership is taken as a sign of bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' looks like a tyrant, but here is one who speaks aloud; METAL, which lead is an example of, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mettle is spirit and pluck, the quality of facing a challenge bravely.

clue.text: Junior doctor discharges English poet

indicators.note: discharges means lets out, so a letter is dropped from the doctor

parts.note: a houseman is the old British term for a junior hospital doctor

explanation.surface: A junior doctor sends an English poet home from hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discharges' takes the E out of HOUSEMAN. A houseman is a British junior hospital doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A. E. Housman was the English poet who wrote A Shropshire Lad.

clue.text: Close to April I put in crop if ground is fertile

indicators.note: put in means placed inside the rearranged letters
ground means crushed up, so crop and if are mixed
close to means the end, so the last letter of April

explanation.surface: Near April someone plants a crop in ground that is fertile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' rearranges the words crop if into PROFIC; 'Close to' takes the last letter of April, and 'put in' places it with I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Prolific means producing in abundance, as fertile land does.

clue.text: Disorderly itinerary of NY-bound Brazilian?

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian city, the home of the traveller in question
someone bound for New York is going to the US

explanation.surface: A messy travel plan for a Brazilian heading to New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The itinerary is RIO TO US: from Rio, going to the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Riotous behaviour is wild and unrestrained, in the manner of a mob causing disorder.

clue.text: Look over independent plant producing mineral

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word for look is read backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word for look, as in lo and behold
a vine is a climbing plant

explanation.surface: Someone inspects an independent factory that produces minerals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory but is a climbing plant; 'over' turns the old word for look round. Lo is an archaic look, as in lo and behold.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivine is a green silicate mineral, found in volcanic rock.

clue.text: Eating out, having this?

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the word eating is scrambled

explanation.surface: A suggestion of what to order when dining at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges EATING. The whole clue also hints at a dish you might order when dining out.
explanation.definitionFit: A tagine is a slow-cooked North African stew, a dish one might well choose in a restaurant.

clue.text: Gong parts sound very unpleasant

indicators.note: parts means splits open, so the honour divides the sound

parts.note: a sound is a noise
a gong is slang for a medal or honour; OM is the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: Parts of a gong make an awful noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gong' looks like the instrument, but is British slang for a medal; the Order of Merit is a British honour. 'parts' means it splits the sound in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or disgusting, especially a smell.

clue.text: Nasty woman has to go on, out of puff

indicators.note: out of means without, so the puff letters are removed

parts.note: to progress is to go on or move forward
PR, public relations, is puff or hype

explanation.surface: An unpleasant woman has to keep going though out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of puff' looks like breathless, but 'out of' removes PR, public relations, from PROGRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogress is a female ogre, used of a cruel or frightening woman.

clue.text: Non-specialist? That covers this, on reflection

definitions.text: Non-specialist? That covers this, on reflection

indicators.note: reflection in a mirror reverses, so the run is read backwards
covers says the word specialist holds the run of letters within it

explanation.surface: Someone unskilled wonders whether a term applies to them when thinking it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That covers this' means the clue's 'specialist' contains the answer: 'covers' finds CIAL in it, and 'on reflection' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Laic means lay, belonging to ordinary people rather than clergy or experts.

clue.text: Fleeing from criminal racket, packing bags randomly

indicators.note: packing means holding inside, so the mixed-up bags pack the other pieces
randomly means the word bags is rearranged in any order

parts.note: con is short for convict, a criminal
a racket is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: A crook runs off from a criminal racket after hastily stuffing bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' looks like a scam but means noise. 'randomly' rearranges the bags to ABSG, and 'packing' puts the criminal and the noise inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to run away secretly, especially to escape arrest.

clue.text: In my opinion, a scholarly book?

definitions.meaning: the phrase '...' means as I see it

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a book seems academic.
explanation.definitionFit: A tome is a large serious book; read as two words, it gives the phrase meaning as far as I am concerned.

clue.text: Lose control, having slipped on pile of new plastic

indicators.note: on means written after the other part
plastic means mouldable, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: slipped means slid

explanation.surface: Someone loses their footing on a heap of new plastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plastic' looks like the material but signals an anagram, turning the words pile of plus N into FLIPONE; 'on' puts the slipping word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To flip one's lid is an idiom for losing one's temper and going wild with rage.

clue.text: Without cover, might still have to pay

indicators.note: removing the cover takes away the outside letters of the word for might

parts.note: might means power or strength

explanation.surface: Even with no insurance cover, someone may still have to pay out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without cover' strips the outer letters from POWER.
explanation.definitionFit: To owe money is to be in debt and obliged to pay it.

clue.text: Conservative Party makes U-turn, being smart

indicators.note: making a U-turn means going back, so the party word is read backwards

parts.note: a revel is a lively party

explanation.surface: The Conservative Party reverses a policy and is called shrewd for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative Party' looks like one name but is two pieces; 'makes U-turn' turns REVEL round.
explanation.definitionFit: Being clever is being intelligent or quick-witted, which smart also means.

clue.text: Woodpile spotted around range

parts.note: a pyre is a pile of wood for burning

indicators.note: around means turned about, so the word for spotted is read backwards

parts.note: spotted means seen

explanation.surface: A heap of wood is noticed somewhere in a stretch of hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' turns the word for spotted round to NEES. 'range' looks like a stove but is the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pyrenees are the mountain range between France and Spain.
